title: Off the expected pattern
core: All four words describe something that fails to match what was expected — a norm, a model, a plan, a starting point. Each needs an implied reference line, and the interesting question is always what that line is and whether leaving it counts as a fault. They split on two axes: whether a judgement is being passed, and whether the reference is a standard you fell short of or a companion you drifted away from.
exam_note: The GRE trades on connotation here: a sentence with "merely," "not necessarily wrong," or "yet to be explained" wants **anomalous**, while one with "troubling," "symptom," or "disciplinary" wants **aberrant** — and **divergent** is the trap answer whenever no shared origin is present.

words.nuance: The only one of the four that convicts. **Aberrant** doesn't just record the mismatch, it treats it as a defect requiring explanation — a pathology, a malfunction, a lapse in conduct. Where the others leave the verdict open, this one has already delivered it.

The judgement-free member of the set. **Anomalous** says only *the model didn't predict this* and deliberately withholds any claim about whether that's bad — the same reading can turn out to be an instrument error or a Nobel Prize. It also presumes the model is right and the case is the odd one, which is exactly the assumption **divergent** never makes.

The verb, and the one that demands a *specified* path to leave — the protocol, the itinerary, the mean, not a vague sense of normalcy. You can be aberrant without anyone naming the standard; you can only **deviate** from something someone laid down. Its connotation is imported, not built in: neutral on a graph, an accusation in an incident report.

Alone in the group, this one involves no norm at all — just two things that started together and are now moving apart, with neither designated the outlier. **Divergent** measures a widening gap between peers (opinions, lineages, roads), so it can't be used for a single specimen that fails a standard the way the other three can.
